title: Speech Order: The Playbook
subtitle: Round Structure · Mission 04
tagline: A debate round has {{cyan:8 speeches}}. Each one has a job. Learn the {{amber:playbook}} and you'll never be the kid asking 'wait — is it my turn?' again. 📋

slides.headline: 📋 OPEN THE MASTER SCHEDULE
body: Think about your regular school day. 🏫 Morning announcements happen **first**. 📝 Math class comes **before lunch**. 🔔 The final bell rings at the **exact same time** every afternoon. Every student and teacher knows {{cyan:exactly}} when it's their turn to move.

Policy debate is the same. A round has **8 speeches**, and every speech has a {{cyan:specific job}} — like positions on a basketball team. The 1A is the {{cyan:starting point guard}}: they bring the ball up first. The 2A is the {{cyan:closer}}: they take the last shot. The Neg players have their own positions too.
Today you learn the playbook. By the end you'll be able to name every speech, in order, and tell which player gives it. 🎯

items.label: Tell Constructive speeches apart from Rebuttal speeches
Match each speech to the right speaker (Debater) (1A / 2A / 1N / 2N)

slides.definition: A {{cyan:constructive}} is a speech where you **build** your arguments. You **read your evidence** and put your case on the table for the first time. 🧱
slides.plainWords: Think: *construction worker*. 👷 You're stacking up the bricks of your argument so the judge can see the whole house.
slides.analogy: Like the {{cyan:opening drive}} of a football game. 🏈 You're not reacting yet — you're setting up the plays. New evidence, new arguments, new ideas all come out here. There are **4 constructive speeches** in a round: 1AC, 1NC, 2AC, 2NC.

slides.definition: A {{amber:rebuttal}} is a speech where you **defend and attack**. You {{amber:can't read new evidence}} — you have to use what's already in the round. ⚔️
slides.plainWords: Think: *lawyer in court*. ⚖️ You're summarizing the strongest parts of your case and tearing down the other team's.
slides.analogy: Like the {{amber:final 2 minutes}} of a basketball game. 🏀 No new players, no new plays — you use the team you've got and the moves you already ran. There are **4 rebuttal speeches** in a round: 1NR, 1AR, 2NR, 2AR.

slides.headline: ⏱️ MEET THE CX PERIOD
slides.intro: Between every constructive speech, there's a **Cross-Examination** — or **CX** for short. 3 minutes where one team asks questions and the other team has to answer. Think of it as the {{cyan:Q&A period}} after a presentation.

cards.name: WHAT IT IS
cards.description: A {{cyan:3-minute Q&A}} that happens right after each of the 4 constructive speeches. You ask, they answer. Then it's their turn to speak.

cards.name: WHEN IT HAPPENS
cards.description: {{cyan:Only after constructives.}} There is **NO CX** between rebuttals. So: 1AC → CX → 1NC → CX → 2AC → CX → 2NC → CX → then straight into the 4 rebuttals.

cards.name: WHO ASKS FIRST
cards.description: The {{amber:2N}} asks the very first CX questions of the whole round (after the 1AC). It's the Negative team's first chance to {{amber:test the Aff's plan}}.

slides.headline: 🎯 THE 8 SPEECHES IN ORDER
slides.intro: Memorize this order. You'll use it every single round. Notice the pattern: **Aff speaks first AND last.** That's not random — it's how the format protects the team carrying the burden of proof.

rows.name: 🧱 CONSTRUCTIVES (1st half of the round)
rows.description: **1AC** → CX → **1NC** → CX → **2AC** → CX → **2NC** → CX. Four big speeches where evidence gets read for the first time. Each one is followed by a 3-minute Q&A.

counter.label: Memory trick
counter.text: **A-N-A-N.** The constructives alternate Aff-Neg-Aff-Neg. The Aff starts (because they have to prove their case). The Neg gets the last constructive (the {{amber:2NC}} — a long attack right before rebuttals start).

rows.name: ⚔️ REBUTTALS (2nd half of the round)
rows.description: **1NR** → **1AR** → **2NR** → **2AR**. Four shorter speeches. {{amber:No CX between rebuttals.}} No new evidence allowed. Just summarizing, defending, and attacking what's already in the round.

counter.label: Memory trick
counter.text: **N-A-N-A.** The rebuttals flip the pattern: Neg-Aff-Neg-Aff. The Neg goes first in rebuttals (the 1NR), but the {{cyan:Aff gets the very last word}} of the entire round (the 2AR). 🎤

rows.name: 🎤 THE BIG PATTERN: AFF SPEAKS FIRST AND LAST
rows.description: The very first speech is the {{cyan:1AC}} (Aff). The very last speech is the {{cyan:2AR}} (Aff). The Aff team **bookends** the entire round.

counter.label: Why it's set up this way
counter.text: The Aff has to *prove* their plan is a good idea — that's a heavier lift than just saying 'no.' So the format gives them the **first word** (to set the case) and the **last word** (to defend it after every attack). Fair trade for carrying the harder burden.

prompt.label: QUICK CHECK
prompt.question: 🧱 What's the **main job** of a constructive speech?

options.text: Build your arguments by reading evidence for the first time
Defend your case and attack the other team's — no new evidence
Pick the winner of the round

correct.title: ✓ FOUNDATIONS POURED
body: Locked in. {{cyan:Constructives}} are where you **build** — you stack up evidence and arguments like a 🧱 construction worker building a house.
correct.followup: **Pro move:** New evidence is *only* allowed in constructives. If a teammate tries to read a fresh card in a rebuttal, the judge can throw it out. Plan accordingly.

b.title: ✕ THAT'S THE REBUTTAL
body: Close, but flipped. {{amber:Defending and attacking with no new evidence}} is the **rebuttal** ⚔️. The **constructive** 🧱 is where you *build* — read fresh evidence and set up your arguments for the first time.

c.title: ✕ THAT'S CX
body: Asking the other team questions is **Cross-Examination** ❓ — the Q&A period *between* constructives. A constructive is the speech itself, not the questions afterward.

d.title: ✕ THAT'S THE JUDGE
body: Picking the winner is the {{amber:judge's}} job ⚖️ — the neutral grown-up in the back of the room. Debaters never pick winners. They just argue.

wrongDefault.title: ✕ MISFIRE
body: The answer is {{cyan:A}}. Constructives 🧱 = **build**. Read evidence. Set up arguments. Rebuttals come later.

slides.intro: Put the **8 speeches** of a policy debate round into the correct speaking order. (Don't worry about the CX periods — just the speeches.)

prompt.label: SEQUENCE LOCK
prompt.question: Drag each speech into the right position, 1st through 8th.

correct.title: ✓ PLAYBOOK LOCKED
body: All 8 in order. The pattern: 4 constructives 🧱 (**A-N-A-N**), then 4 rebuttals ⚔️ (**N-A-N-A**). The {{cyan:Aff bookends the round}} — they speak first (1AC) and last (2AR).
correct.followup: **Pro move:** When you sit down at the table, write the 8-speech order at the top of your flow paper *before the round starts*. It anchors you all round long.

wrongDefault.title: ✕ REORDER REQUIRED
body: Two patterns to lock in: **Constructives go A-N-A-N** (1AC, 1NC, 2AC, 2NC). Then **rebuttals flip to N-A-N-A** (1NR, 1AR, 2NR, 2AR). The Aff always starts the round and always ends it.

prompt.label: PHASE CHECK
prompt.scenario: You're at a debate tournament. 🏆 Each speech below is happening in some round somewhere right now. Drop each one into the right bin.
prompt.question: Sort each speech as a Constructive 🧱 or a Rebuttal ⚔️.

correct.title: ✓ TWO PHASES SORTED
body: Clean. Every speech name tells you which bin it's in: if it ends in **C**, it's a {{cyan:Constructive}} 🧱. If it ends in **R**, it's a {{amber:Rebuttal}} ⚔️.
correct.followup: **Memory trick:** *C is for Construct. R is for Rebut.* The number tells you which speaker (1 or 2) and the letter in the middle tells you the team (A or N).

wrongDefault.title: ✕ PHASE CONFUSION
body: Look at the **last letter** of each speech name. **C = Constructive** 🧱 (build, read evidence). **R = Rebuttal** ⚔️ (defend, no new evidence). 1AC ends in C → constructive. 1NR ends in R → rebuttal.

prompt.label: SQUAD ASSIGNMENT
prompt.scenario: Every debater on a 2-person team has **two speeches** to give in a round. Match each player to the pair of speeches they're responsible for.
prompt.question: Drag from the left to the matching speech pair on the right.

correct.title: ✓ SQUAD ASSIGNED
body: Clean match. The pattern is simple: your **number** sticks with you. If you're {{cyan:1A}}, you give the 1AC and the 1AR. If you're {{cyan:2A}}, you give the 2AC and the 2AR. Same on the {{amber:Neg}} side.
correct.followup: **Pro move:** Talk to your {{cyan:Debate Partner}} *before* the season starts about who wants 1 vs. 2. The 1A opens (lots of pressure). The 2A closes (lots of pressure of a different kind). Pick the role that fits your strengths.

wrongDefault.title: ✕ MIXED UP THE ROLES
body: The trick: **your number sticks with you**. 1A = 1AC + 1AR. 2A = 2AC + 2AR. 1N = 1NC + 1NR. 2N = 2NC + 2NR. Each debater gives one constructive and one rebuttal — *their own number's pair*.

prompt.label: PATTERN CHECK
prompt.question: 🎤 Which team gets to speak **both first AND last** in a policy debate round?

options.text: Whichever team won the coin flip

correct.title: ✓ BOOKEND CONFIRMED
body: Locked in. The {{cyan:Aff}} opens the round with the **1AC** and closes it with the **2AR**. They bookend the entire debate. 📚
correct.followup: **Why it's set up this way:** the Aff has the {{cyan:burden of proof}} — they have to *prove* their plan is good, which is a harder job than just saying 'no.' Giving them the first and last word is a fair trade for that heavier lift.

b.title: ✕ FLIPPED
body: The {{amber:Neg}} speaks a lot in the middle (1NC, 2NC, 1NR, 2NR) but they don't bookend. The {{cyan:Aff}} opens with the **1AC** and closes with the **2AR**.

c.title: ✕ NO COIN FLIP
body: Policy debate doesn't use a coin flip for speech order. The order is **always the same**: 1AC first, 2AR last. The {{cyan:Aff bookends}} every round.

d.title: ✕ NOT EXACT ALTERNATION
body: The teams don't perfectly alternate. The Negative gets two speeches in a row in the middle (the {{amber:2NC → 1NR}} block — called the *Neg Block*). And the {{cyan:Aff}} gets both the first *and* the last word.

wrongDefault.title: ✕ MISFIRE
body: The answer is {{cyan:A — Affirmative}}. The 1AC is the first speech of the round. The 2AR is the last. Both Aff.

prompt.label: BUILD ORDER
prompt.scenario: Fill in the missing words to describe the shape of a policy debate round.
prompt.question: Drop the right word into each blank.

slides.template: A policy debate round has two phases. First come the four {{1}} speeches, where each team **builds** their arguments and reads new evidence. Then come the four {{2}} speeches, where teams **defend and attack** what's already in the round. Between each constructive there's a 3-minute {{3}} period where one team asks the other questions.

blanks.hint: The 🧱 phase — where evidence gets read for the first time
The ⚔️ phase — no new evidence, just defending and attacking
Three letters or the full term — the ❓ Q&A period

correct.title: ✓ ROUND ASSEMBLED
body: That's the whole shape: four {{cyan:Constructives}} 🧱 → four {{amber:Rebuttals}} ⚔️, with a {{cyan:CX}} ❓ Q&A after each constructive. Eight speeches, four Q&As, one round.

wrongDefault.title: ✕ REBUILD
body: Three terms to lock in: {{cyan:Constructive}} 🧱 (build with new evidence), {{amber:Rebuttal}} ⚔️ (defend and attack, no new evidence), {{cyan:Cross-Examination}} ❓ (the 3-min Q&A after each constructive).

prompt.label: BIG IDEA CHECK
prompt.scenario: Your {{cyan:Debate Partner}} 🤝 leans over in round 2 and whispers: *'Wait — I'm the 1A this round. Quick: what's the biggest difference between a constructive and a rebuttal? I have like 10 seconds.'*
prompt.question: 🎯 What's the **clearest** one-line answer you can give them?

options.text: Constructives are longer, rebuttals are shorter — that's the only difference.
You can read new evidence in constructives. You can't in rebuttals.
Aff gives all the constructives. Neg gives all the rebuttals.
There's no real difference — just two names for speeches.

correct.title: ✓ THAT'S THE WHOLE GAME
body: Exactly. The **rule about evidence** is what makes the two phases different. {{cyan:Constructives}} 🧱 = new evidence allowed (build the house). {{amber:Rebuttals}} ⚔️ = no new evidence (defend what you've already built).
correct.followup: **Pro tip:** This means you have to be *strategic* about what evidence you read and *when*. Save your strongest cards for the constructive where they'll do the most damage — because if you forget, you can't bring them back later.

a.title: ✕ LENGTH ISN'T THE BIG IDEA
body: It's true rebuttals are shorter — but that's not the *core* difference. The big rule is about **evidence**: constructives 🧱 let you read new evidence; rebuttals ⚔️ don't. *That's* what separates the two phases.

c.title: ✕ BOTH TEAMS DO BOTH
body: Both teams give both kinds of speeches. {{cyan:Aff}} gives 1AC and 2AC (constructives) AND 1AR and 2AR (rebuttals). {{amber:Neg}} does the same. The difference between constructive and rebuttal is about **evidence**, not which team is talking.

d.title: ✕ HUGE DIFFERENCE
body: There's a *massive* difference. {{cyan:Constructives}} 🧱 let you bring in new evidence and new arguments. {{amber:Rebuttals}} ⚔️ don't — you work with what's already in the round. That rule shapes the whole strategy of a debate.

wrongDefault.title: ✕ MISFIRE
body: The answer is {{cyan:B}}. The big rule: **new evidence is allowed in constructives, not in rebuttals.** That's the line that separates the two phases.

slides.headline: PLAYBOOK: MEMORIZED ✅
slides.subtext: You know the order. {{cyan:1AC → 1NC → 2AC → 2NC}} (constructives 🧱), then {{amber:1NR → 1AR → 2NR → 2AR}} (rebuttals ⚔️). The {{cyan:Aff}} bookends. Every player has two speeches. CX ❓ comes after every constructive. You're ready for round 1. 🎤
